name: Nausea Or Vomiting
preview_text: The smell, timing, and triggers of your nausea tell a TCM practitioner exactly which organ system is out of balance - and most patterns respond to herbs and acupuncture within two ...
synonyms: ["Feeling Sick Or Vomiting", "Nausea And Vomiting", "Nausea or tendency to vomit", "Functional nausea and vomiting", "Nausea and vomiting (various causes)", "Vomiting or nausea with inability to eat"]
conventional_description: Nausea is an unpleasant sensation of needing to vomit, while vomiting is the forceful expulsion of stomach contents. These symptoms can arise from many causes: gastroenteritis, food poisoning, motion sickness, pregnancy, migraines, medication side effects, or emotional distress. Diagnosis relies on a careful history and physical exam, sometimes supported by blood tests or imaging when a more serious underlying condition is suspected.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management often includes antiemetic drugs such as ondansetron, metoclopramide, or promethazine, along with dietary adjustments (the BRAT diet - bananas, rice, applesauce, toast) and oral rehydration solutions. When nausea is a side effect of other medications, the dose may be adjusted or the drug changed. In pregnancy or after surgery, specific protocols are followed to minimize risk.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the Stomach is the central pivot of digestion. Its job is to receive food and send it downward - a movement called Stomach Qi descending. When that downward movement fails, Qi rebels and rises, bringing nausea and vomiting. So the immediate problem is always rebellious Stomach Qi, but the real question is what caused it to rebel.
The trigger can be something the Stomach cannot process, like a heavy, greasy meal that sits and ferments (Food Stagnation). It can be an emotional storm - frustration or anger that makes Liver Qi attack the Stomach, forcing it to churn upward. It can be a sticky accumulation of Dampness and Heat, or a cold, watery buildup of Phlegm-Fluids that drowns the digestive fire. And sometimes the problem isn't an excess at all, but a deficiency: a Stomach that has lost its warming Yang and can no longer move anything downward, or a Stomach so dry and Yin-deficient that it cannot guide food along.
This is why a TCM practitioner asks so many questions about the vomit itself. Sour, foul-smelling vomit that brings relief points to Food Stagnation. Vomiting of thin, watery fluid with a splashing sound in the belly suggests Phlegm-Fluids. Dry retching with a parched mouth signals Yin Deficiency. The trigger - stress, cold, overeating - and the tongue and pulse confirm the pattern. What Western medicine calls "nausea and vomiting" TCM sees as six different landscapes, each needing its own map.
classical_quote: 「伤寒五六日，中风，往来寒热，胸胁苦满，默默不欲饮食，心烦喜呕……小柴胡汤主之。」

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner begins by asking what the nausea feels like, when it strikes, and what the vomit looks and smells like. The quality and timing of the symptom are the first clues that point toward one pattern rather than another. A sudden onset after a heavy meal tells a very different story from a chronic, low‑grade queasiness that worsens with fatigue or stress.
When nausea strikes shortly after overeating and the vomit is sour and foul‑smelling, the picture points to Food Stagnation in the Stomach. The person feels a bloated, uncomfortable fullness in the upper abdomen. The tongue coating is thick and greasy, and the pulse feels slippery. This pattern signals a digestive backlog that needs clearing rather than an underlying weakness.
If nausea flares during stress or frustration, and is joined by belching, acid reflux, and a distended feeling along the ribs, the root is often Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach. The tongue edges may look red, and the pulse has a taut, wiry quality. The emotional trigger and the rib‑side discomfort are the key signs that separate this from simple indigestion.
Vomiting of watery, thin fluid and a sensation of heaviness or fullness in the chest suggest Phlegm‑Fluids accumulating in the Stomach. The tongue typically has a white, greasy coating, and the pulse is slippery. This pattern often arises when fluid metabolism is sluggish, so the practitioner will ask about a history of digestive dampness or a feeling of foggy heaviness.
When nausea comes with a sticky taste, a heavy body sensation, and a stuffy fullness, Damp‑Heat in the Stomach is a likely culprit. The tongue is red with a thick, yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse feels slippery and rapid. This pattern often follows rich, greasy foods or hot, humid weather. The yellow coating and rapid pulse confirm that Heat is present alongside Dampness.
Chronic, low‑grade nausea with vomiting of clear fluid and cold hands and feet points to Stomach Yang Deficiency with Cold. The tongue appears pale with a white coating, and the pulse is slow and weak. In contrast, dry retching, a burning sensation in the stomach, and nausea that worsens in the afternoon suggest Stomach Yin Deficiency. Here the tongue looks red and peeled, with a thin and rapid pulse.

patterns.symptoms: ["Vomiting of sour, undigested food that relieves bloating", "Epigastric fullness and distension worse after eating", "Belching with a sour, rotten odour", "Aversion to food and its smell", "Thick, greasy or curd-like tongue coating"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating, Greasy, fried foods, Cold, raw foods, Dairy, Lying down after meals
patterns.better_with: Vomiting (temporary relief), Fasting or skipping a meal, Warm water, Gentle walking, Light, easily digested food
patterns.why_this_happens: When you overeat or consume rich, greasy foods, the Stomach struggles to break them down and move them onward. The undigested food sits and ferments, producing sour-smelling gas and acid. This blockage forces Stomach Qi to rebel upward instead of descending, resulting in nausea and vomiting of sour, foul-smelling food that brings temporary relief from the bloated pressure.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal body with a thick, greasy or curd-like coating, thickest in the centre. Pulse: slippery (Hua) and full, especially at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overeating and heavy, greasy foods overwhelm the Stomach's digestive capacity, causing food to stagnate and ferment. This blockage forces Stomach Qi upward, resulting in nausea and vomiting. Vomiting temporarily expels the stagnant matter, relieving the pressure. Fasting and light, warm foods allow the Stomach to process the backlog, while gentle movement helps Qi descend and aids digestion. Lying down after eating, on the other hand, allows food to sit and ferment, worsening the stagnation and nausea.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat smaller, lighter meals and avoid greasy, fried, or hard-to-digest foods. Chew thoroughly and stop eating before you feel full. Gentle walking after meals helps digestion, but avoid lying down right after eating.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach
patterns.symptoms: ["Nausea and vomiting triggered by emotional stress", "Belching and acid reflux", "Distending pain that radiates to the rib area", "Irritability and frequent sighing", "Sensation of a lump in the throat"]
patterns.worse_with: Anger or frustration, Fatty, greasy foods, Alcohol, Skipping meals or eating late, Stressful situations
patterns.better_with: Stress reduction and relaxation, Warm, bland meals, Gentle exercise like walking, Deep breathing exercises
patterns.why_this_happens: Emotional stress, frustration, or anger causes the Liver Qi to stagnate. Instead of flowing smoothly, this stuck Qi attacks the Stomach, reversing its normal downward movement. The result is rebellious Stomach Qi rising upward, producing nausea, vomiting, and sour belching, often with a tight, distending sensation in the rib area.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red body with redder sides, thin white coating. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), especially at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress causes Liver Qi to stagnate, which then attacks the Stomach and forces Qi upward, leading to nausea and vomiting. Fatty and greasy foods further burden the digestive system and promote stagnation. Relaxation and gentle movement help smooth the flow of Liver Qi, while bland, regular meals allow the Stomach to recover its downward-moving function.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, regular meals of bland, easily digestible foods like congee and steamed vegetables. Avoid greasy, spicy, and fried foods that can aggravate Liver Qi. Practice stress-reducing activities like gentle yoga, walking, or meditation. Avoid eating when upset.

patterns.pattern_name: Phlegm-Fluids in the Stomach and Small intestine
patterns.symptoms: ["Vomiting of thin, clear watery fluid", "Splashing water sound when moving or tapping the abdomen", "Feeling of fullness and hardness below the chest", "No thirst, or thirst without desire to drink"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, raw, and greasy foods, Damp or humid weather, Overeating or large meals, Lying down immediately after eating
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the abdomen, Sipping warm ginger tea, Gentle walking after meals, Resting in a semi-upright position
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen's ability to transform and transport fluids is weakened, fluids accumulate and turn into Phlegm-Fluids. These fluids lodge in the Stomach, blocking its normal downward movement and forcing Stomach Qi to rebel upward, which produces nausea and vomiting of thin, watery fluid. The trapped fluids also create the characteristic splashing sounds and a heavy, full sensation in the upper abdomen.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen, with teeth marks and a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep (沉 chén), wiry (弦 xián), and slippery (滑 huá), especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and damp foods or environments add to the body's internal dampness and cold, further impairing Spleen Yang and promoting Phlegm-Fluid accumulation. Warmth and ginger tea counteract the cold and help the Spleen transform fluids, while gentle movement encourages Qi flow and prevents stagnation. Resting upright allows gravity to assist Stomach Qi in descending, reducing the urge to vomit.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked meals and avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that create dampness. Sip ginger tea to warm the stomach and reduce nausea. Gentle walking after meals aids digestion and prevents fluid stagnation. Keep the abdomen warm and dry.

patterns.symptoms: ["Nausea with a sticky, greasy taste in the mouth", "Feeling of heaviness in the body and limbs", "Thirst with little desire to drink", "Yellow, greasy, thick tongue coating", "Upper belly fullness and stuffiness"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or rich foods, Alcohol or sweet drinks, Hot, humid weather, Overeating or eating late at night, Spicy foods
patterns.better_with: Light, bland foods (congee, steamed greens), Warm, cooked meals, Gentle movement after meals, Drinking warm water or barley tea, Keeping regular meal times
patterns.why_this_happens: Dampness and Heat combine in the Stomach, creating a heavy, sticky obstruction that prevents Stomach Qi from descending. This trapped Qi then rebels upward, causing nausea and vomiting. The Dampness brings a sensation of heaviness and a greasy taste, while the Heat adds a burning discomfort and thirst that isn't relieved by drinking.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen with red prickles in the centre; thick, yellow, greasy coating. Pulse: slippery (滑 Huá) and rapid (数 Shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat is sticky and heavy. Greasy, sweet, or spicy foods and alcohol directly add more Dampness and Heat to the Stomach, worsening the obstruction and making nausea worse. A light, bland diet is easier to digest and doesn't create extra dampness. Warm, cooked foods support the Stomach's ability to transform and transport, helping Dampness resolve. Gentle movement encourages Qi to move downward, relieving the stuck, bloated feeling.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, rich, and spicy foods, as well as alcohol and sweet drinks - they create more Dampness and Heat. Eat light, easily digestible meals like congee, steamed vegetables, and barley. Drink warm water or barley tea. Gentle movement after meals helps Qi flow, and keeping a regular eating schedule supports the Stomach's rhythm.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dull, cold pain in the upper belly that improves with warmth and pressure", "Vomiting of clear watery fluid", "Cold hands and feet", "Preference for hot food and drinks", "Tiredness and lack of energy"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold or raw foods, Iced drinks, Overeating or large meals, Cold weather or drafts, Stress and worry
patterns.better_with: Warm food and drinks, A warm compress on the belly, Rest and lying down, Small, frequent meals, Ginger tea
patterns.why_this_happens:
Your Stomach acts like a cooking pot that needs a steady fire to digest food and send it downward. When Stomach Yang-the digestive fire-runs low, coldness accumulates inside. The Stomach then loses its ability to move Qi downward; instead it rebels upward, causing nausea and vomiting of clear, watery fluid.
This cold-deficiency state also weakens the Spleen's ability to transform fluids, so water builds up in the stomach. The nausea is chronic, often worse after cold foods or when you feel chilled, and it improves with warmth and gentle pressure on the belly.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks; white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, slow, weak, especially in the right Guan (Stomach) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work:
Cold and raw foods require more digestive fire to process, which a Yang-deficient Stomach simply doesn't have. They directly worsen the internal cold, triggering nausea and vomiting. Large meals overwhelm the weakened digestive system, causing food to stagnate and Qi to rebel upward.

Warmth, on the other hand, temporarily restores the digestive fire. Warm liquids like ginger tea gently stimulate Yang and help the Stomach settle. Rest conserves Qi, and small meals avoid overburdening the system. A warm compress directly delivers heat to the middle burner, easing the cold pain and allowing the Stomach to resume its downward movement.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat only warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees. Avoid all cold, raw, and iced items. Sip warm ginger tea throughout the day. Apply a warm compress or hot water bottle to your upper belly after meals. Eat small, frequent portions and rest after eating.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dry retching with little or no vomit", "Thirst for small sips, dry mouth and throat", "Burning or gnawing discomfort in the stomach", "Red tongue with little or no coating, dry centre"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy, fried, or drying foods, Alcohol and coffee, Late nights and overwork, Emotional stress and worry, Hot, dry weather
patterns.better_with: Cool, moist air, Small sips of warm water, Moist, bland foods (congee, pear), Rest and avoiding overwork
patterns.why_this_happens: The Stomach relies on Yin fluids to stay moist, cool, and able to guide food downward. When those fluids run low, the Stomach becomes dry and overheated, losing its grip on descending Qi. That rebellious Qi pushes upward, causing dry retching and nausea - often with little or nothing to bring up - along with a gnawing, burning emptiness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red with little or no coating, dry centre. Pulse: fine (Xi) and rapid (Shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stomach Yin is like the cooling, moistening fluid that keeps the digestive engine running smoothly. When it runs low, the engine overheats and Qi rebels upward. Spicy, fried foods and alcohol act like throwing fuel on a fire, further burning up Yin and worsening dryness and nausea. Rest and moistening foods help refill that reservoir, while small sips of water provide just enough moisture to settle the Stomach without overwhelming it. Stress and overwork consume Yin, so calming the mind and body directly protects the fluids that keep the Stomach descending comfortably.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods, as well as alcohol and coffee. Eat small, frequent meals of moist, bland foods like rice congee, pear, and steamed vegetables. Sip warm water throughout the day rather than gulping large amounts. Prioritize rest, keep late nights to a minimum, and practise gentle, calming activities such as walking or yin yoga to preserve fluids.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture stop vomiting immediately?
faqs.answer: For many people, yes - especially when the nausea is acute and the underlying pattern is excess in nature. The point Pericardium-6 (Neiguan, on the inner wrist) is famous for calming rebellious Stomach Qi and can be needled or pressed during an episode. In a clinical setting, acupuncture often reduces the urge to vomit within minutes. Chronic nausea may take a few sessions to settle fully.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs with my anti-nausea medication?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, but you should always tell both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor what you are taking. Herbs that descend Stomach Qi, such as Ban Xia (Pinellia), are commonly used alongside conventional antiemetics without issue. If your medication causes drowsiness, your practitioner will avoid herbs with strong sedative properties. Never stop prescribed medication suddenly - work with your doctor to adjust doses as your symptoms improve.

faqs.question: What can I eat when everything makes me nauseous?
faqs.answer: Start with the simplest, most neutral foods: plain congee (rice porridge), a slice of dry toast, or a few sips of warm ginger tea. Ginger is a classic TCM remedy that gently warms the Stomach and directs Qi downward. Avoid cold, raw, greasy, and dairy-heavy foods, which are harder to digest. Eat tiny amounts frequently rather than large meals, and rest in a semi-upright position after eating.

faqs.question: I vomit whenever I get stressed. Can herbs really help?
faqs.answer: Yes - this is a textbook Liver Qi invading the Stomach pattern. The formula Xiao Chai Hu Tang (Minor Bupleurum Decoction) with Zuo Jin Wan (Left Metal Pill) soothes the Liver, clears heat, and sends rebellious Stomach Qi downward. Many patients notice that within a few weeks, their gut feels less reactive to emotional triggers. Acupuncture at points like Taichong (Liver-3) and Neiguan (PC-6) reinforces this calming effect.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with morning sickness?
faqs.answer: TCM has a long tradition of treating nausea in pregnancy, and our dedicated Morning Sickness page goes into detail on the specific patterns involved. The core principle is the same - calming rebellious Stomach Qi - but the herbal choices are carefully selected to be safe for both mother and baby. Always consult a qualified practitioner rather than self-prescribing during pregnancy.

faqs.question: Are there acupressure points I can use at home?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pericardium-6 (Neiguan) is the most famous anti-nausea point. Find it three finger-widths below the wrist crease, between the two tendons on the inner forearm. Press firmly with your thumb for two to three minutes while breathing slowly. Stomach-36 (Zusanli), four finger-widths below the kneecap and one finger-width outside the shinbone, is also useful for strengthening digestion. These points are safe to use as often as needed.

faqs.question: What if I can't keep the herbs down?
faqs.answer: This is a common concern. Your practitioner can adjust the formula to be gentler on the Stomach or prescribe it as a tea sipped very slowly in tiny amounts. Some patients start with acupuncture alone to settle the vomiting first, then introduce herbs once the Stomach is calmer. In severe cases, the herbs can be administered as a retention enema or through acupoint injection, though this is less common.

research.title: Stimulation of the wrist acupuncture point P6 for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting
research.description: This Cochrane review assessed the effectiveness of P6 acupoint stimulation for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting. It found that P6 stimulation significantly reduced the risk of nausea and vomiting compared to sham treatment, with a risk ratio comparable to antiemetic drugs.
research.periodical: Lee A, Fan LTY. Stimulation of the wrist acupuncture point P6 for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2009;(2):CD003281.

research.title: Acupuncture-point stimulation for chemotherapy-induced nausea or vomiting
research.description: This Cochrane review evaluated acupuncture-point stimulation for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. The review concluded that electroacupuncture and acupressure at P6 reduced the incidence of acute vomiting, with acupressure also reducing nausea severity.
research.periodical: Ezzo J, Richardson MA, Vickers A, et al. Acupuncture-point stimulation for chemotherapy-induced nausea or vomiting. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2006;(2):CD002285.

research.title: Acupuncture to treat nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: This randomized controlled trial compared traditional acupuncture at PC6 with sham acupuncture for nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy. Women receiving real acupuncture had significantly less nausea and dry retching, supporting acupuncture as a safe, effective option.
research.periodical: Smith C, Crowther C, Beilby J. Acupuncture to treat nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy: a randomized controlled trial. Birth. 2002 Mar;29(1):1-9.
